description: We are a team of two from Sapporo, Japan. Our leader has spent 17 years as an astronomy instructor, stargazing with children. A child who sees the Moon through a telescope says “Wow!”, but the feeling fades within days. And the spacecraft left on the Moon and Mars cannot be seen at all. The Next Explorers is our answer: a card game that starts from the real sky and leads children into the stories of NASA’s spacecraft. We want to turn one night of “Wow!” into a lasting “I want to know more!”
summary:
The Next Explorers is a web app that lets children aged 8 to 12 discover NASA’s spacecraft through play. It features 19 spacecraft sent to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

Children first hold a phone up to the sky to find the Moon or Mars. Choosing that world opens the stories of the spacecraft that went there. After reading, they answer quizzes to level up their cards, then use what they have learned to take on a boss battle.

Each story explains what the machine is, why it was sent, and what it found. Every story ends with the same question: “Where is it now?” Surveyor 3, for example, fell silent in 1967 and still sits in the Moon’s Ocean of Storms. Every chapter cites a NASA source.

Our team leader has spent 17 years as an astronomy instructor in Sapporo, Japan, stargazing with children. A child who sees the Moon through a telescope says “Wow!”, but the feeling fades within days. And spacecraft cannot be seen through a telescope at all. By linking the real sky to the machines left there, we want to turn one night of wonder into lasting curiosity.
details:
What it is

A card game for children in grades 3 to 6 (ages 8 to 12) that runs in a web browser. There is nothing to install, and it can be played in Japanese or English.

  1. Find it in the sky: Hold a phone up to the sky to see where the Moon or Mars is right now.
  2. Read the story: Choose a spacecraft that went to that world and read its short, photo-illustrated story.
  3. Answer the quiz: The quiz questions come from the story.
  4. Level up the card: Correct answers raise the card’s level and unlock more NASA photos.
  5. Battle the boss: Build a team from the cards you have raised and take on a boss.

How it addresses the challenge

The challenge asks us to explain what the equipment left behind is, why it was sent, and what discoveries it made possible. Each story in the app follows that order.

  • What it is and why it was sent: Surveyor 3 was a robotic lander sent to study the lunar surface before people landed on the Moon.
  • What it found: Phoenix confirmed water ice beneath the Martian soil. InSight recorded 1,319 marsquakes.
  • Where it is now: All 19 stories end with the spacecraft’s location, its current status, the date of its last contact, and what remains.
  • What we still do not know: Each story closes with an open question that has no single right answer. Children are invited to think it through for themselves.

Of the 19 spacecraft, 14 appear in the challenge Resources (6 on the Moon, 7 on Mars, 1 in deep space). The app clearly separates hardware that remains on the surface, spacecraft that were destroyed on entering an atmosphere, and missions that are still operating.

What makes it creative

Star map apps show the sky. NASA’s websites explain the spacecraft. This app connects the two. Children start from the real Moon above their heads, move into the story of the machine left there, and then into a game. The moment a child realizes “it is still sitting up there,” the spacecraft becomes something close to them.

The boss battles are part of the learning too. Each card’s skill is based on a real instrument or event. Spirit’s skill, “Discovery in a Pinch,” comes from a true story: a wheel that had stopped working dragged through the soil and uncovered a clue to ancient water.

How we kept it accurate

  • Sources: All 79 chapters and all 139 learning facts cite a NASA source, so adults can check them for themselves.
  • Saying so when we do not know: Dates that could not be confirmed in the record are marked “unconfirmed.”
  • Separating fact from game: Bosses and levels are game settings. The app explains that the bosses are fictional and do not mean that life has been found.
  • Readable for children: The Japanese version uses mostly hiragana and short sentences.
  • Safe to play: There are no ads, no purchases, and no online multiplayer. Progress and notes are stored only in the browser.

Intended impact

The interest sparked at a stargazing event usually ends that same night. With this app, children can keep playing after they go home. Because it opens in a browser and supports Japanese and English, it can be used in schools, science museums, and stargazing events in other countries.

During these two days, we were not able to have children try the app. Our next step is to use it at stargazing events, improve it based on how children respond, and add more spacecraft.

Tools and data

  • Development and hosting: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, deployed as an HTTPS web app using Lolipop Deploy Now.
  • NASA references: NASA Science mission pages and NSSDCA support the mission histories, equipment descriptions, scientific findings and status information. NASA Open Data catalogue entries provide additional archive references; we do not claim independent analysis of those raw datasets.
  • Images and videos: 172 NASA-sourced still-image assets and five official videos from the NASA Image and Video Library, JPL Photojournal, Scientific Visualization Studio and NASA-hosted partner resources. Original media and image-processing credits are retained. These source images and videos were not generated by SI.
  • Surface locations: NASA lunar landing-site records and MER traverse records from Washington University’s NASA/PDS-related Analyst’s Notebook support historical locations and rover routes, not live tracking.
  • Sky direction: Astronomy Engine 2.1.19 (MIT licence) calculates azimuth and altitude from the observing time and location. The AR overlay is an approximate guide to the Moon and planets; it does not detect spacecraft or show their precise current positions.
  • Preparation and testing: Team-provided quiz spreadsheets were curated against linked NASA references. Python, openpyxl, Pillow and FFmpeg supported data and media preparation; Node.js and LinkeDOM supported automated software tests.
  • Super Intelligence (SI) assistance: ChatGPT, OpenAI Codex and Claude Code assisted with research, coding, debugging, game design, educational writing, content checking and Japanese–English translation. Google Translate supported early translation drafts. SI-assisted educational text and game graphics are project adaptations, not NASA-authored or NASA-endorsed materials. The app uses prewritten content and does not generate new scientific explanations during play.

Detailed references and individual media credits are available in the app’s Sources and NASA Data & Resources screens.
